# Write a file, read it back, count the words
text = """the quick brown fox
jumps over the lazy dog
the dog barks"""

with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(text)

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    lines = f.read().splitlines()

counts = {}
for line in lines:
    for word in line.split():
        counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1

for word, n in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:5]:
    print(f"  {word:<6} {n}")

lesson.title: Log processing in a deploy script
lesson.note: wc, awk, sort, uniq and grep compose into a pipeline — the everyday shell toolkit.
lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Build a small log file, then process it the way a deploy script would
cat > deploy.log <<'EOF'
2026-03-11 10:02 INFO  build started
2026-03-11 10:04 INFO  tests passed
2026-03-11 10:05 WARN  cache miss
2026-03-11 10:06 ERROR push rejected
2026-03-11 10:07 INFO  retrying
2026-03-11 10:08 INFO  deploy complete
EOF

echo "== line count =="
wc -l < deploy.log

echo
echo "== counts by level =="
awk '{print $3}' deploy.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

echo
echo "== anything that went wrong =="
grep -E 'WARN|ERROR' deploy.log || echo 'clean run'

echo
echo "== exit status check =="
if grep -q ERROR deploy.log; then
  echo 'pipeline would fail here'
else
  echo 'pipeline green'
fi

lesson.title: Round-robin scheduling
lesson.note: Each process gets a fixed quantum before being sent to the back of the queue — the basis of time-sharing.
lesson.code:
# Round-robin scheduling with a quantum of 3
jobs = [("P1", 7), ("P2", 4), ("P3", 9), ("P4", 2)]
quantum, clock = 3, 0
remaining = dict(jobs)
queue = [name for name, _ in jobs]
finish = {}

while queue:
    name = queue.pop(0)
    slice_ = min(quantum, remaining[name])
    print(f"t={clock:>2}  run {name} for {slice_}")
    clock += slice_
    remaining[name] -= slice_
    if remaining[name]:
        queue.append(name)
    else:
        finish[name] = clock

print()
total = 0
for name, burst in jobs:
    turnaround = finish[name]
    total += turnaround
    print(f"{name}  burst {burst}  finished at {finish[name]:>2}  turnaround {turnaround}")
print(f"\naverage turnaround: {total/len(jobs):.2f}")

lesson.title: Hashing and the avalanche effect
lesson.note: One changed character rewrites roughly half the digest bits — and chaining hashes gives you a blockchain.
lesson.code:
import hashlib

def sha(text):
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()

# One changed character avalanches through the whole digest
a, b = "open computer science", "open computer scienca"
ha, hb = sha(a), sha(b)

print(f"{a!r}\n  {ha}")
print(f"{b!r}\n  {hb}")

diff = sum(x != y for x, y in zip(bin(int(ha,16))[2:].zfill(256), bin(int(hb,16))[2:].zfill(256)))
print(f"\n{diff} of 256 bits differ ({diff/256:.1%})")

# A three-block chain, each block committing to the one before
prev = "0" * 64
for i, payload in enumerate(["alice->bob 5", "bob->carol 2", "carol->dan 1"], 1):
    prev = sha(prev + payload)
    print(f"block {i}  {payload:<14} {prev[:32]}...")

lesson.title: Proof of work, and why tampering fails
lesson.note: Each block commits to the hash before it, so changing old data invalidates everything after it.
lesson.code:
import hashlib, time

def sha(text):
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()

def mine(index, prev, data, difficulty=4):
    target = "0" * difficulty
    nonce = 0
    while True:
        h = sha(f"{index}{prev}{data}{nonce}")
        if h.startswith(target):
            return nonce, h
        nonce += 1

chain = [{"index": 0, "prev": "0" * 64, "data": "genesis", "nonce": 0,
          "hash": sha("genesis")}]

for i, data in enumerate(["alice->bob 5", "bob->carol 2", "carol->dan 1"], start=1):
    prev = chain[-1]["hash"]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    nonce, h = mine(i, prev, data)
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    chain.append({"index": i, "prev": prev, "data": data, "nonce": nonce, "hash": h})
    print(f"block {i}  {data:<14} nonce {nonce:>7}  {h[:20]}...")

valid = all(chain[i]["prev"] == chain[i-1]["hash"] for i in range(1, len(chain)))
print(f"\nchain length {len(chain)}, links valid: {valid}")

chain[1]["data"] = "alice->bob 500"       # tamper with one block
recomputed = sha(f"{1}{chain[1]['prev']}{chain[1]['data']}{chain[1]['nonce']}")
print(f"after tampering, block 1 hash matches: {recomputed == chain[1]['hash']}")

lesson.title: Fitting a line by least squares
lesson.note: The closed-form solution recovers the slope and intercept that generated the data, even through the noise.
lesson.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 60)
y = 2.4 * x + 1.7 + rng.normal(0, 1.5, x.size)

X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
w = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]

pred = X @ w
r2 = 1 - ((y - pred) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()

print(f"intercept : {w[0]:.3f}   (true 1.700)")
print(f"slope     : {w[1]:.3f}   (true 2.400)")
print(f"R^2       : {r2:.4f}")

lesson.title: Backpropagation from scratch
lesson.note: A 2-4-1 network learns XOR with no framework at all — just matrix multiplies and the chain rule.
lesson.code:
import numpy as np

# A 2-2-1 network learning XOR, written out by hand
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.array([[0,0],[0,1],[1,0],[1,1]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([[0],[1],[1],[0]], dtype=float)

sig  = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
dsig = lambda a: a * (1 - a)

W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)), np.zeros((1, 4))
W2, b2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)), np.zeros((1, 1))

for epoch in range(1, 4001):
    h  = sig(X @ W1 + b1)
    out = sig(h @ W2 + b2)
    loss = ((out - y) ** 2).mean()

    d2 = (out - y) * dsig(out)
    d1 = (d2 @ W2.T) * dsig(h)
    W2 -= 0.5 * h.T @ d2;  b2 -= 0.5 * d2.sum(0, keepdims=True)
    W1 -= 0.5 * X.T @ d1;  b1 -= 0.5 * d1.sum(0, keepdims=True)

    if epoch % 1000 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:>4}   loss {loss:.6f}")

print()
for xi, p in zip(X, sig(sig(X @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2)):
    print(f"  {int(xi[0])} XOR {int(xi[1])} -> {p[0]:.4f}")

lesson.title: Sobel edge detection from scratch
lesson.note: Convolving an image with two small kernels is all edge detection is — no library required.
lesson.code:
import numpy as np

# A synthetic 12x12 image: dark background, bright square in the middle
img = np.zeros((12, 12))
img[3:9, 3:9] = 1.0

# Sobel kernels detect intensity change in x and y
Kx = np.array([[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=float)
Ky = Kx.T

def convolve(a, k):
    h, w = a.shape
    out = np.zeros((h - 2, w - 2))
    for i in range(h - 2):
        for j in range(w - 2):
            out[i, j] = (a[i:i+3, j:j+3] * k).sum()
    return out

gx, gy = convolve(img, Kx), convolve(img, Ky)
mag = np.sqrt(gx**2 + gy**2)

print("edge magnitude map (blank = flat, # = edge):")
for row in mag:
    print("  " + "".join("#" if v > 1 else "." for v in row))

print(f"\nedge pixels : {(mag > 1).sum()} of {mag.size}")
print(f"max response: {mag.max():.2f}")

lesson.title: Tokenising and TF-IDF by hand
lesson.note: A term matters when it is frequent in one document and rare across the rest. That is the whole formula.
lesson.code:
import math, re
from collections import Counter

docs = [
    "the cat sat on the mat",
    "the dog sat on the log",
    "cats and dogs are pets",
]

tokenise = lambda t: re.findall(r"[a-z]+", t.lower())
tokens = [tokenise(d) for d in docs]

print("tokens per document:")
for i, t in enumerate(tokens):
    print(f"  doc{i}: {t}")

# inverse document frequency, then tf-idf by hand
N = len(docs)
df = Counter(w for t in tokens for w in set(t))

print("\ntop tf-idf terms per document:")
for i, t in enumerate(tokens):
    tf = Counter(t)
    scores = {w: (c / len(t)) * math.log(N / df[w]) for w, c in tf.items()}
    top = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:3]
    pretty = ", ".join(f"{w} {s:.3f}" for w, s in top if s > 0)
    print(f"  doc{i}: {pretty}")
